subject: The U.S. Foreclosure Map Is Shifting
body_text:

 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 Follow the Fed: Bank of Japan raises rates to highest level since 1995 .

 State approval: Are the Saudis next to take possession of the F-35? 

 Huang forecast: Nvidia ( NVDA ) set to double chip volume next year.


 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 Moving up the coast 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
 It used to be the foreclosure capital of the United States, but no longer. Florida has been officially replaced as the chief repossession hub as South Carolina takes the top spot, according to  fresh data from real estate analytics firm ATTOM. The state registered one foreclosure for every 1,547 housing units, more than double the national average, with three of its metropolitan areas—Columbia, Spartanburg, and Charleston—ranking among the top five worst-affected metros nationwide.

 What happened? Florida held the definitive title of having the nation's highest foreclosure rate through most of 2025 and 2026. Keeping it on top of the list was increasing financial distress in the Sunshine State related to surging homeowners' insurance premiums, as well as runaway condo association and development fees. However, the pressures are now moving north to the Palmetto State amid a shifting economic landscape.

The hardest-hit areas of South Carolina are military markets with high concentrations of VA loans, which allow buyers to purchase homes with zero money down. Given elevated borrowing costs ( and now going higher ), alongside continuous spikes in prices for gas and utilities, these areas are feeling serious budget strains. Current foreclosure filings are also concentrated among people who bought homes from 2022 onward, triggering a negative equity trap as home prices flattened out.

 Outlook: While the spike in South Carolina suggests some distress in the local market, the broader American housing market is widely intact, and foreclosure volumes remain below historical norms. The real estate picture is still difficult given cooling home sales, with high interest rates that make buyers think twice and many locked-in sellers unwilling to budge on price. Expect a structural reset to continue in the coming years as housing reverts to its historical role as a slow-appreciating asset rather than a fast-track wealth generator.
